title: Someone else's explanation
text: Why can you understand an idea, yet struggle to use it? Often, you haven't really understood it for yourself. Someone else has simply explained it in a way that makes it feel clear.

title: Three signs of an illusion
text: While you're learning something, you may feel you understand it completely. But when you face a real problem, one of three things happens. You draw a blank. You don't even realize that something you've learned could help, as if you'd never learned it at all. Or you stumble through a few vague keywords, perhaps remembering them incorrectly. Or you sound perfectly convincing, offering one solution after another, while the problem remains completely unchanged. This is the illusion of understanding, a common experience in learning.

title: Borrowing the author's structure
text: When you learn by reading a textbook or watching a tutorial, you're actually borrowing the author's structure of knowledge to make sense of the subject.

title: The work the author has already done
text: The author already understands the subject deeply. They know what matters, what can be left out, what must stay, and why. They know what to explain first, and what should come next. So the information you receive is clearly expressed, with well-chosen examples, tightly connected reasoning, and language that's easy to follow.

title: Mistaking fluency for understanding
text: That makes reading feel effortless. But it feels effortless because the author has worked hard to explain things in the easiest possible way for you to understand. Your brain has an instinctive shortcut: if something is easy to process, I probably understand it already. So when the reading flows smoothly, your brain reaches the wrong conclusion: I understand this now.
